content: Fuchsine, also known as rosaniline hydrochloride, is a magenta-colored dye with the chemical formula C20H19N3·HCl. When dissolved in water, it exhibits a magenta hue, while in its solid state, it forms dark green crystals. This compound is not only used for dyeing textiles but also serves as a bacterial stain and, in some cases, as a disinfectant. The name fuchsine originates from its first manufacturer, Renard frères et Franc. The etymology of the name is typically attributed to two sources: the color of the flowers of the plant genus Fuchsia, which was named in honor of the botanist Leonhart Fuchs, or the German translation of the French word Renard, meaning fox. An article published in Répertoire de Pharmacie in 1861 suggested that the name was chosen to reflect both of these reasons. Acid fuchsine is a derivative of basic fuchsine, modified by the addition of sulfonic groups. This modification results in a mixture of homologues, yielding twelve possible isomers. Despite slight variations in their properties, all of these isomers are considered satisfactory for use. Basic fuchsine itself is a mixture of rosaniline, pararosaniline, and Magenta II. For applications such as the preparation of Schiff reagent, formulations with a high content of pararosaniline are required. However, the exact composition of basic fuchsine can vary depending on the manufacturer and production batch, which can influence its suitability for specific purposes. When basic fuchsine is combined with phenol as an accentuator, it is referred to as carbol fuchsin. This formulation is particularly used for staining Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis.
